0.title: Jonah: Salvation Belongs to the LORD
0.overview:
The message. Jonah is the story of a God whose mercy is larger than his servant’s heart. God sends his prophet to warn Nineveh, the great city of Israel’s cruellest enemy, and Jonah runs the other way, because he knows exactly what God is like: “a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster” (4:2). God pursues him through storm and sea, rescues him, sends him again, and spares the city when it repents. The heart of the book is Jonah’s cry from the deep, “Salvation belongs to the LORD!” (2:9): salvation is God’s to give, to a runaway prophet and to a violent city alike. The book ends with a question God asks and Jonah never answers, left for every reader who is glad of mercy for himself but not for his enemies.

Background: the prophet. Jonah son of Amittai was a real prophet of the northern kingdom of Israel, from Gath-hepher in Galilee. Kings records that Jeroboam II won back Israel’s lost territory “according to the word of the LORD, the God of Israel, which he spoke by his servant Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet” (2 Kings 14:25). Jeroboam reigned about 793 to 753 BC, so Jonah worked in the early eighth century BC, around the time of Amos and Hosea.

Who wrote it, and when. The book does not name its author. Many older interpreters thought Jonah wrote it himself, an honest record of his own failure. Many modern scholars place it after the exile, pointing to some words that look late and to 3:3, which says Nineveh “was” a great city, as if it were gone. Neither point settles the matter: such words could be heard in northern Israel long before the exile, and a storyteller naturally says “was” of the time of his story. This commentary takes the events to have happened in Jonah’s lifetime, about 760 BC, and sees nothing that requires a late date; who set it down we do not know.

The world of the book. Assyria was the rising power of the age, and Nineveh, on the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, was one of its great royal cities and later its capital. The Assyrians were notorious for cruelty; Nahum would call Nineveh “the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder” (Nahum 3:1). In Jonah’s day the empire was weakened by revolts and plague, and a total eclipse of the sun was recorded in 763 BC, events that may have left the city ready to listen. In 722 BC Assyria destroyed Jonah’s own kingdom and carried its people away (2 Kings 17:6). This was the enemy Jonah was sent to warn. Instead he sailed from Joppa for Tarshish, probably in Spain: as far the other way as a ticket could take him.

What kind of book it is. Jonah stands among the twelve shorter prophets, yet it is not a collection of sermons but a story about a prophet, whose one recorded sermon is a single sentence: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!” (3:4). It is told with great skill and irony, and includes a psalm of thanks woven from the Psalms (2:2–9). Everything in it obeys God at once (wind, sea, fish, plant, worm, pagan sailors, a pagan city) except the one man who knows him best. Read it as true history told by a skilful storyteller, and expect it, at the end, to turn round and face you.

Is Jonah history? Some Christians read the book as a parable because of the great fish and the repentance of a whole city of which Assyrian records say nothing; Jesus, they suggest, could refer to Jonah as a preacher refers to a well-known story. They are right that the message is the point. But the book is written as plain narrative about a named prophet whom Kings places in real history. And Jesus does more than mention it: “The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah” (Matthew 12:41). Characters in a parable cannot stand up at the Last Day to condemn real people, and he sets the Ninevites beside the queen of the South, who was certainly real (Matthew 12:42).

This commentary’s view. Jonah is history, chiefly because Jesus treated it so, and his word is decisive for us. A great fish is no difficulty for the God who raised Jesus from the dead, and the silence of Assyrian records is no surprise: kings recorded victories, not repentance. Details such as the size of the city (3:3) remain debated and are discussed where they arise.

How the book makes its case. The story falls into two matching halves, each opening with the word of the LORD to Jonah (1:1; 3:1). In the first (chapters 1–2) Jonah runs. God hurls a storm after him, and the sailors who throw him overboard end up fearing the LORD and offering him sacrifice (chapter 1). God appoints a great fish, and from inside it Jonah prays at last and is brought back to dry land (chapter 2). In the second (chapters 3–4) the word comes “the second time” (3:1), and Jonah obeys. Nineveh believes God, from the king down, and turns “from the violence that is in his hands” (3:8), and God relents, as he said he would when a nation turns (Jeremiah 18:7–8). Then Jonah is furious, and God answers him with a plant, a worm, a scorching wind and a question (chapter 4). In each half outsiders respond to God better than his prophet, and God shows mercy to the undeserving. The last word is God’s: “And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city …?” (4:11).

Where it leads: to Christ. Jesus made Jonah a sign of his death and resurrection: “For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). So the book points to Christ by pattern: a man thrown into the deep that others might live, and brought back by God. But Jesus also said, “something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41), and the differences teach as much. Jonah slept through a storm he had caused; Jesus stilled the storm with a word (Mark 4:39). Jonah went into the deep for his own sin; Jesus went into death for ours, and rose. Jonah sat on a hillside hoping a city would burn; Jesus looked at a city that had rejected him and “wept over it” (Luke 19:41), then died for his enemies: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). And the gracious God of 4:2, whose mercy always reached beyond Israel, is seen in full in Christ: Jonah’s compassion stopped at his own border; Christ’s did not.

For us. Jonah is uncomfortable reading for religious people. Timothy Keller often pointed out that Jonah plays both sons in Jesus’ parable of the lost son: the younger who runs from the father, and the elder who sulks outside when the father welcomes a sinner home (Luke 15:28). The gospel meets both. Because salvation belongs to the LORD, no runaway is beyond his pursuit, and failure is not the end of usefulness: the word comes a second time. Because it is all grace, given to us while we were enemies, we have no ground to begrudge it to anyone. The church is sent to its own Ninevehs with a better message than Jonah’s, that “repentance for the forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in his name to all nations” (Luke 24:47). God’s question is still open, and our lives answer it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Call and the Flight
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet who knows God best runs from him, and every step he takes is downward. God’s command is plain and urgent: arise, go to Nineveh, the great city whose evil has come up before him, and call out against it (vv. 1–2). Jonah rises, but to flee, heading west for Tarshish when God sent him east, and the narrator marks the stages of his descent: down to Joppa, down into the ship (v. 3). Twice we are told that he is going “from the presence of the LORD”, and the rest of the chapter shows how impossible that is.
verseByVerse.theology: God sends his word to a city that deserves judgment, and his own prophet runs the other way.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the word of the LORD came to Jonah the son of Amittai, saying, "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it, for their evil has come up before me." But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD. He went down to Joppa and found a ship going to Tarshish. So he paid the fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sends his prophet to warn the cruellest city of the age, and Jonah deliberately runs the other way, out of God’s service.

Jonah the son of Amittai. Jonah, from the Galilean village of Gath-hepher, had earlier announced that Jeroboam II would restore Israel’s borders (2 Kings 14:25), good news for Israel. This message is different, and Jonah will hate it.

Nineveh, that great city. The Assyrians were famous for cruelty (see the introduction); Nahum would call Nineveh “the bloody city, all full of lies and plunder” (Nahum 3:1), and Assyria would eventually destroy Jonah’s own country (2 Kings 17:6). Preaching there was like carrying a warning to the headquarters of an enemy army that had burned your neighbours’ villages.

Their evil has come up before me. Jonah is sent to announce judgment. The Hebrew word for “evil” can also mean “disaster” (ESV note), and it runs right through the book: Nineveh’s evil here, the “evil” that comes on the ship (v. 7), the disaster God relents from (3:10), and the evil that rises in Jonah’s own heart when he does (4:1).

Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish. God said “Arise, go”; Jonah “rose to flee”. Nineveh lay hundreds of miles east, overland; Tarshish lay far west across the Mediterranean, probably in Spain. The reason waits until the end, where Jonah gives it himself: he knew God was gracious and feared Nineveh would be spared (see the note on 4:1–3). Watch the word “down”. Jonah goes down to Joppa, down into the ship, down into the inner part of it (v. 5), down into the sea, and down “to the roots of the mountains” (2:6). Sin always leads downward, one step at a time, and every step feels like freedom. And he “paid the fare”: running from God always costs something.

From the presence of the LORD. Jonah knew that God fills heaven and earth; he says so in verse 9. He was not looking for a place beyond God’s reach. He was resigning, walking out of God’s service.

The Son who did not run. Jonah fled a hard errand. The Son of God was sent on a far costlier one, knowing it would end in a cross, and “he set his face to go to Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51). He said, “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

Running today. We cannot escape God’s presence: “If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me” (Psalm 139:9–10). But we can stop praying, stop meeting with God’s people, and put distance between ourselves and the thing God has told us to do. The God who pursues Jonah through this chapter pursues such runaways too, to bring them home.

Where Christians differ. Some Christians read Jonah as a parable, because of the fish and the sudden repentance of a whole city; most of the church, including the Reformed tradition, has read it as history.

This commentary’s view. Jonah is history, chiefly because Jesus treated it so. He compared Jonah’s time in the fish with his own death and resurrection, and said that the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment to condemn his hearers (Matthew 12:39–41); the characters of a parable cannot do that. Either way, the message is aimed squarely at the reader (see the introduction).
verseByVerse.note: Jonah son of Amittai prophesied under Jeroboam II (about 780 BC). Nineveh stood on the Tigris, opposite modern Mosul in Iraq; Joppa is modern Jaffa.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God will not let his servant go, and he uses a storm, a pagan crew and a lot to bring him into the light. The LORD hurls a great wind; the sailors pray and throw the cargo overboard while Jonah sleeps below, until the captain wakes him with God’s own words, “Arise, call out” (vv. 4–6). The lot falls on Jonah, and under questioning he confesses the God who made the sea and the dry land, the very God he is fleeing (vv. 7–9). The pagans see the madness of it before the prophet does (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: There is no running from God, and a believer's disobedience puts others in the storm with him.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD hurled a great wind upon the sea, and there was a mighty tempest on the sea, so that the ship threatened to break up. Then the mariners were afraid, and each cried out to his god. And they hurled the cargo that was in the ship into the sea to lighten it for them. But Jonah had gone down into the inner part of the ship and had lain down and was fast asleep. So the captain came and said to him, "What do you mean, you sleeper? Arise, call out to your god! Perhaps the god will give a thought to us, that we may not perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God hurls a storm after his runaway prophet, and while pagan sailors pray for their lives, the one man who knows the true God sleeps.

But the LORD hurled a great wind. The first “But” was Jonah’s (v. 3); this one is God’s, and it settles the matter. God “hurled” the wind, as a man hurls a spear. The storm is not bad luck but the pursuit of a runaway by the God who will not let him go. Say it plainly: this storm is mercy. God could have let Jonah sail away.

The mariners were afraid. Experienced sailors were terrified, which shows how bad the storm was. They did two sensible things: they prayed, “each” to “his god”, and they hurled the cargo overboard, sacrificing their profit to save their lives.

Had lain down and was fast asleep. Pagans pray while the one man who knows the true God sleeps through a crisis he caused, a contrast both deliberate and damning. Spiritual sleep is like that: the further we run from God, the less we feel the danger.

Arise, call out to your god! Now a pagan captain has to tell a prophet to pray, in the very words God used in verse 2, “Arise … call out”. God’s command catches up with Jonah in the mouth of an unbeliever. It is humbling when an unbeliever shames a Christian into doing what God had already commanded, and worth listening when they do.

Two sleepers. Christians think at once of another boat in another storm, where Jesus lay “asleep on the cushion” while his disciples panicked (Mark 4:38). But the two sleepers are opposites. Jonah slept in rebellion, and the storm was his fault; Jesus slept in perfect peace, and then “rebuked the wind” so that “there was a great calm” (Mark 4:39). Jonah must be thrown overboard to save the crew; Jesus speaks and saves them all. As the disciples asked, “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?” (Mark 4:41).

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to one another, "Come, let us cast lots, that we may know on whose account this evil has come upon us." So they cast lots, and the lot fell on Jonah. Then they said to him, "Tell us on whose account this evil has come upon us. What is your occupation? And where do you come from? What is your country? And of what people are you?" And he said to them, "I am a Hebrew, and I fear the LORD, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land." Then the men were exceedingly afraid and said to him, "What is this that you have done!" For the men knew that he was fleeing from the presence of the LORD, because he had told them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God exposes Jonah through the lot, and the prophet’s flawless confession of the Creator condemns his flight from him.

Come, let us cast lots. Casting lots was the ancient way of putting a question to heaven, and God directs the answer: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (Proverbs 16:33). God has closed in on Jonah through wind, waves and now a pebble in a sailor’s hand.

What is your occupation? The questions tumble out, and both who Jonah is and what he does condemn him. The honest answer to “What is your occupation?” was: a prophet of God, running away from God.

I fear the LORD. Jonah’s answer is perfectly orthodox and painfully ironic. He says “I fear the LORD” while running from him. He confesses that God “made the sea and the dry land”, the very two places he has been using as an escape route: the sea he is sailing on and the dry land he came from.

What is this that you have done! The sailors are more shocked than Jonah. Their cry is horror, not a question: they see what a believer half-asleep in his sin cannot, that running from the Maker of sea and land is madness.

Because he had told them. Jonah had mentioned his flight as if it were ordinary news. Sin talked about casually is still sin, and the people around us usually understand that better than we do.

Sunday’s creed and Monday’s life. You can hold a completely correct doctrine of God and live as if none of it were true. Before shaking our heads at Jonah, we should ask what we confess on Sunday and contradict on Monday. None of us lives up to our creed; only Christ ever did, and his perfect obedience is credited to all who trust him. So the gap between what we believe and how we live, once confessed, becomes a place to receive mercy, and his Spirit begins to close it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One man goes into the sea, the storm is stilled, and those who were perishing come to fear the LORD. Jonah tells the crew to throw him overboard, admitting that the storm is his fault (vv. 11–12). They row hard to spare him, then pray to the LORD and do as he said, and the sea stops raging (vv. 13–15). Sailors who began the night crying to their own gods end it sacrificing to the LORD (v. 16). And the God who rules the sea appoints a great fish, so that what looks like the end of Jonah is his rescue (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: God saves pagan sailors through the sin of his prophet, and saves the prophet himself by a fish.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said to him, "What shall we do to you, that the sea may quiet down for us?" For the sea grew more and more tempestuous. He said to them, "Pick me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down for you, for I know it is because of me that this great tempest has come upon you." Nevertheless, the men rowed hard to get back to dry land, but they could not, for the sea grew more and more tempestuous against them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jonah at last admits that the storm is his fault and offers his life for the crew, while the pagan sailors risk their own lives to spare him.

It is because of me. Jonah’s first honest act: he owns the fault and offers his life for the crew. Some read it as repentance, some as despair, a man who would rather drown than go to Nineveh; both may be true at once. Even now he does not offer to pray, or to turn round and obey.

The men rowed hard. Rather than throw him overboard, the sailors rowed hard (the Hebrew says they “dug”, ESV note, digging in their oars), risking their own lives to save the man who had endangered them. In chapter 4 Jonah will be furious that God saves a city. The people we write off often show more compassion than we do.

One man for the many. God is doing more here than Jonah understands. One man is thrown into the deep so that many are saved, and the storm falls silent. Centuries later Caiaphas said, without knowing what he was saying, “it is better for you that one man should die for the people” (John 11:50). Jonah is a reluctant, half-hearted picture of the willing Saviour: “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). The difference is that Jonah deserved the storm and Jesus did not.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they called out to the LORD, "O LORD, let us not perish for this man's life, and lay not on us innocent blood, for you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you." So they picked up Jonah and hurled him into the sea, and the sea ceased from its raging. Then the men feared the LORD exceedingly, and they offered a sacrifice to the LORD and made vows.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The sailors turn from their own gods to the LORD, and when the sea falls calm they worship him: the first converts in the book are pagans.

Therefore they called out to the LORD. In verse 5 each cried out to his god; now they call on the LORD, the covenant name of the God of Israel. Their prayer is careful: do not hold us guilty of “innocent blood”; and they own that the storm was God’s doing: “you, O LORD, have done as it pleased you.” They have learned more theology in one night than some learn in a lifetime.

Hurled him into the sea. This is the fourth “hurl” of the chapter. God hurled the wind, the sailors hurled the cargo, Jonah told them to hurl him, and now they hurl the prophet. The moment he hits the water, the sea is still. When the cause of the storm is dealt with, the storm is over.

The men feared the LORD exceedingly. Afraid of the storm before, now they fear the LORD, with sacrifice and vows: reverence, worship and commitment. The first conversion in the book is of pagan sailors, not Israelites.

The fear in the other boat. When Jesus stilled the sea, the disciples made the same turn: “they were filled with great fear” (Mark 4:41), not of the storm, which was gone, but of the LORD of the sea sitting in the boat with them.

Through a disobedient prophet. God did this through a disobedient prophet who never preached them a sermon. He is not limited by his servants’ failures, though that is no excuse for failing. If anyone thought the message of this book was “God loves Israel and judges the nations”, the first chapter has already corrected it: salvation is reaching foreigners in the middle of the sea while the prophet sinks.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD appointed a great fish to swallow up Jonah. And Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God appoints a great fish to swallow Jonah: what looks like the end of the runaway is his rescue, and a sign of Christ’s death and resurrection.

The LORD appointed a great fish. The word “appointed” is a key to the rest of the book. Later God appoints a plant, a worm and a scorching wind (4:6–8). He commands the whole creation, great and small, to deal with one stubborn man. (The ESV notes that the verb may be read “had appointed”, which would mean the fish was already on its way before Jonah hit the water.)

A fish, not a whale. Scripture says “a great fish”, not a whale, and the point is not biology but sovereignty: the sea Jonah used as an escape route has become God’s instrument. Amos said the same in his own way: even at “the bottom of the sea” God can reach a runaway (Amos 9:3).

A sign of Christ. Jesus said, “just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). Jonah went into the deep because of his own sin; Jesus went into death because of ours. Jonah was spat out on the shore; Jesus rose in glory. And he added words that should make every reader tremble: “something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41).

What the fish really was. It looks like the end of Jonah; it is his rescue. God’s strangest providences are often his kindest. Many believers can look back at some dark swallowing time, the illness, the failure, the collapse, and say that it was the fish God sent to save them.

Could a man survive in a fish? It was a miracle: the LORD “appointed” the fish, and Jesus spoke of it as real (Matthew 12:40). For many modern readers this is where Jonah becomes a children’s tale. But notice what that assumes. If there is no God, of course no fish was appointed, but then the question was settled before we opened the book. If there is a God who “made the sea and the dry land” (1:9), a fish in the right place is no great strain, and the resurrection Jesus pointed to is far greater (see the note on John 2:11–12).

The fish is not the hard part. People stumble over the fish and pass over what is truly outrageous here: that God loves Nineveh, the cruellest city of its age, and spares it when it turns. Every culture finds that harder to believe than any miracle, because every culture has its Ninevehs, people it is sure are beyond mercy. A fish costs God nothing. Grace to his enemies is the miracle that cost him something, and in the end it cost him his Son.

How do three days and three nights fit Jesus’ death on Friday and rising on Sunday? Jews counted any part of a day as a day and night (compare 1 Samuel 30:12–13; Esther 4:16 with 5:1). Friday afternoon, Saturday and early Sunday are three days; Jesus also said he would be raised “on the third day” (Matthew 16:21).
verseByVerse.note: In the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 2, so Jonah 1:17 is 2:1 there (ESV note).

1.title: Fleeing from the Presence of the LORD
1.overview:
Where we are. The book opens with nothing but a name and a command. Jonah son of Amittai, a prophet who had once brought Israel good news (2 Kings 14:25), is sent to Nineveh, a great city of Israel’s most feared enemy (see the introduction).

The message. No one can run from the God who made the sea and the dry land, and he pursues his runaways because he means to show mercy. The prophet who knows God best flees from him, while pagans who hardly know him end up fearing and worshipping him. God’s purposes are not stopped by his servant’s disobedience, and his mercy is reaching beyond Israel before Nineveh has heard a word.

Why it was said. Israel under Jeroboam II was prosperous and proud of its privileges, inclined to treat God’s favour as its own possession, while Assyria rose as the enemy on the horizon (see the introduction). The chapter confronts a people who, like Jonah, could recite the right creed while refusing God’s errand to the nations.

How the chapter makes its case. The call and the flight (vv. 1–3): God says “Arise, go”, and Jonah rises to flee, going down to Joppa and down into a ship bound the other way. The storm (vv. 4–10): God hurls a great wind after him; the sailors pray while the prophet sleeps, the lot picks him out, and his flawless confession of the Creator condemns his flight. The sea (vv. 11–17): Jonah tells them to throw him overboard; they row hard to spare him, then pray to the LORD and do it, and the sea falls still. The sailors offer sacrifice to the LORD, and God appoints a great fish to swallow his prophet.

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern, as Jesus himself taught: one man goes into the deep, the storm is stilled and the others are saved, and the swallowed prophet becomes “the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matthew 12:39), pointing to the Son of Man’s three days in the heart of the earth. The contrasts teach as much. Jonah slept through a storm of his own making and had to be thrown; Jesus slept in peace, stilled the storm with a word, and went willingly into the deep of judgment, “the righteous for the unrighteous” (1 Peter 3:18).

For us. We cannot outrun God, and we should be glad of it, because the storm that chases a runaway is mercy, not malice. Ask where you are buying a ticket for Tarshish, and remember that the one who went into the deep for you has already stilled the storm you deserved.
1.theology:
God's call comes to his servants on his terms, and includes the people we would rather he left alone (vv. 1-2).

No one can escape God's presence; disobedience is a downward road, and it is never free (v. 3; Ps 139:7-10).

God rules wind, sea, lots and fish, and he pursues his straying servants with providences that feel like disasters and are actually mercies (vv. 4, 7, 17; Prov 16:33).

A believer's sin drags others into the storm, and outsiders often see it more clearly than he does (vv. 5-6, 10).

Correct doctrine held by a disobedient heart is worthless; faith is shown by obedience (vv. 9-10).

One man is thrown into the deep so that others may live: a dim picture of Christ, who suffered the righteous for the unrighteous (vv. 12, 15; John 11:50; 1 Pet 3:18).

God saves whom he will, even pagan sailors through a failing prophet, and the fish itself is rescue, not punishment (vv. 16-17; Matt 12:40-41).
1.examples:
Jonah buys a ticket in the opposite direction and falls asleep below deck while unbelievers pray, until a pagan captain has to tell him to say his prayers. A creed can be recited perfectly by a man who is running away from it, and the people around us often see that before we do.

The sailors dig in their oars to save the man who endangered them, and the sea falls silent the moment he is in the water. Then comes a fish that looks like the end and turns out to be the rescue. God's strangest providences can be his kindest, even when we have brought the storm on ourselves.

keyVerse.quote: But Jonah rose to flee to Tarshish from the presence of the LORD.
keyVerse.note: God has just said “Arise, go”, and his prophet rises to flee. Everything else in the chapter, every step down and every wave God hurls after him, answers the question this verse raises: can anyone run from the presence of the LORD? The answer is no, and the good news is that the God who will not let his runaways go came after us himself in his Son.

1.reflection:
Jonah ran not because he doubted God but because he knew him (4:2). Where are you tempted to avoid something God has plainly asked of you, and what are you afraid will happen if you obey?

The narrator traces Jonah’s path down to Joppa, down into the ship and down into its hold (vv. 3, 5). How does running from God usually look in ordinary life: not a dramatic rebellion, but small steps of distance? What helps someone notice the direction early?

Jonah confesses the God “who made the sea and the dry land” (v. 9) while fleeing across the sea. Where might there be a gap between what we confess on Sunday and how we live on Monday, and how does the gospel meet us in that gap?

Jesus called himself greater than Jonah (Matthew 12:41). Compare Jonah asleep in the storm and thrown into the sea with Jesus asleep in the boat and going to the cross (Mark 4:35–41). What do the differences show you about him?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Out of the Belly of Sheol
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even from the depths, the one who calls on the LORD is heard, and only God can bring him up. Jonah prays at last, from inside the fish, and his prayer is mostly thanksgiving, looking back on the moment he went under: he called, and God answered (vv. 1–2). He sees God’s hand behind the sailors’ hands: God cast him into the deep, and God’s waves passed over him (v. 3). Driven from God’s sight, he still hopes to see the temple again (v. 4). The waters close, the weeds wrap round him, and the bars of death shut, until God reverses everything: “Yet you brought up my life from the pit” (vv. 5–6).
verseByVerse.theology: From the lowest place a believer can fall, God hears prayer and lifts him out.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God from the belly of the fish, saying, "I called out to the LORD, out of my distress, and he answered me; out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From inside the fish Jonah prays at last, thanking God that when he cried out from the very edge of death, God heard him.

Then Jonah prayed to the LORD his God. Jonah did not pray on the ship, even when the captain told him to (1:6). It sometimes takes the bottom of the sea to make a believer pray.

Two small phrases. First, “the LORD his God”. After all his running, God is still his God: Jonah let go of God, but God did not let go of him. Second, “from the belly of the fish”. No place is so dark or so strange that prayer cannot reach God from it.

Out of the belly of Sheol I cried. The prayer is mostly a song of thanks, looking back on the moment he went under. Sheol is the realm of the dead: Jonah was as good as dead when he cried, and God “answered” and “heard”.

In the words of the Psalms. The Psalms echo all through this prayer: “In my distress I called upon the LORD … From his temple he heard my voice” (Psalm 18:6). Jonah prays in the words of Israel’s hymnbook. When we are too frightened or ashamed to find words of our own, God’s words become our prayer, and a believer who has filled his mind with Scripture in calm days will find it there in the dark.

Did Jonah die in the fish? His prayer uses the Psalms’ language of being at death’s door (Psalm 18:4–5). Most readers take it that he was preserved alive; either way, he came up from the depths as a sign of the one who would rise from the dead.
verseByVerse.note: The opening line echoes Ps 120:1, In my distress I called to the LORD, and he answered me, and v. 4 echoes Ps 31:22, I am cut off from your sight.

verseByVerse.quote: For you cast me into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the flood surrounded me; all your breakers and your waves passed over me. Then I said, 'I am driven away from your sight; yet I shall again look upon your holy temple.' The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me; weeds were wrapped about my head. To the roots of the mountains I went down, to the land whose bars closed upon me forever. Yet you brought up my life from the pit, O LORD my God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jonah sees that God himself cast him into the deep, and that when he had sunk past all hope, God himself brought him up.

You cast me into the deep. The sailors threw Jonah overboard (1:15), at his own suggestion, but he prays, “you cast me into the deep”. He sees God’s hand behind the sailors’ hands, as the psalmist did: “all your breakers and your waves have gone over me” (Psalm 42:7).

I am driven away from your sight. Jonah had tried to flee “from the presence of the LORD” (1:3); now, sinking, his fear is that he has been driven from God’s sight. We discover how much we want God when we think we have lost him.

Yet I shall again look upon your holy temple. Then faith speaks its “yet”. Israelites prayed towards the temple in Jerusalem, where God had promised to hear his people (1 Kings 8:38–39), and Jonah believes he will stand there again. This is faith in its barest form: no evidence, no way out, only the confidence that God will not abandon him.

To the roots of the mountains I went down. Water closes over his head, weeds tangle round him, and he sinks past “the roots of the mountains”. The “bars” are the gates of the world of the dead, shutting behind him “forever”. Here the journey downward that began at Joppa (1:3) reaches its end.

Yet you brought up my life from the pit. Then the second “Yet”. The direction is finally reversed, and God is the one who reverses it, as the psalm says: “O LORD, you have brought up my soul from Sheol” (Psalm 30:3). A man cannot climb back up from the roots of the mountains. He can only be carried.

The one who was not left there. On the day of Pentecost Peter took another psalm of rescue from the pit and applied it to Jesus: “For you will not abandon my soul to Hades, or let your Holy One see corruption” (Acts 2:27). Jonah was brought up from the edge of death; Christ went all the way into it and was raised, and everyone joined to him will be carried up too.

What this does not mean. “You cast me” is not fatalism, and it excuses no one’s wrongdoing. It is the comfort of knowing that nothing reaches us except through God’s hand. A Christian in a hospital bed or a collapsing business is not in the grip of blind chance.

Uncertain wording. The small Hebrew word translated “yet” in verse 4 can be read, with different vowels, as “how”, and some translations (such as the NRSV) take the line as despair: “how shall I look again upon your holy temple?” The ESV’s reading, a word of faith, fits the rising movement of the psalm, and either way verse 7 shows that his prayer did reach the temple.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–10 — Salvation Belongs to the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Salvation is God’s gift, not our achievement, and everything else people trust is empty beside it. As his life ebbed away Jonah remembered the LORD, and his prayer reached God’s holy temple (v. 7). Those who cling to empty idols abandon the steadfast love that could have been theirs (v. 8), but Jonah will give thanks, offer sacrifice and keep his vows, for “Salvation belongs to the LORD!” (v. 9). God has only to speak, and the fish gives the prophet back to the dry land, where obedience can begin again (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation is God's to give, not ours to earn or to ration out to the people we approve of.

verseByVerse.quote: When my life was fainting away, I remembered the LORD, and my prayer came to you, into your holy temple. Those who pay regard to vain idols forsake their hope of steadfast love. But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you; what I have vowed I will pay. Salvation belongs to the LORD!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
As his life ebbed away Jonah remembered the LORD, and he confesses that idols are empty and that rescue is God’s alone to give.

I remembered the LORD. Jonah had not forgotten that God exists; he had been living as if God did not matter. Remembering, in the Bible, means turning the whole attention back to God and acting on it. And from the bottom of the sea his prayer reached God’s “holy temple”.

Those who pay regard to vain idols. An idol is anything we trust to do for us what only God can do, and it is always empty. Those who cling to such things walk away from the one love that would never fail them.

A sting for Jonah. Jonah’s words are right, and there is a sting in them he may not have felt. He had just watched pagan sailors abandon their gods and worship the LORD (1:16), while he, who knew better, had run away. The truth we preach has a way of turning round to face us.

Salvation belongs to the LORD! The prayer ends with the sentence that holds the whole book together, a line straight out of the Psalms (Psalm 3:8). Rescue is not something we achieve, arrange or deserve. It is God’s, and he gives it as he pleases. Jonah now promises what the sailors did on deck (1:16): sacrifice and vows.

Two things in the prayer. Jonah gives thanks before he is rescued; he is still inside the fish. That is real faith, thanking God for a deliverance he cannot yet see. But for all its beauty, the prayer never actually confesses the flight, and it never mentions Nineveh. A man can pray a thoroughly biblical prayer and still hold on to the very thing God is dealing with, and chapter 4 will show that this is what has happened.

The New Testament echo. The New Testament says the same in other words: “For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). And in heaven the cry goes up from a countless crowd from every nation: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10).

The exhausting work of saving ourselves. Few people today use the word salvation, but almost everyone seeks it under other names: becoming who I really am, the right partner, financial freedom, the right side of history. Our age hands the whole job to the individual, to make yourself, justify yourself and keep proving it, and many are quietly crushed by the load. Religion can be the same project in church clothes: if I pray enough and behave well enough, God will have to accept me. Jonah, at the bottom of the sea, has run out of both options. He cannot climb, bargain or prove anything, and only there does he learn the sentence that ends the striving. It is not a motto for the strong but good news for the sunk. The one who went down into the deep for us has done the saving, and what is left for us is to receive it, and rest.

The harder test. Jonah means these words about himself. It is easy to celebrate them when salvation comes to us; in chapter 4 he will find it much harder when it comes to Nineveh.

Uncertain wording. Verse 8 is compressed. The Hebrew says that idol-worshippers “forsake their steadfast love”, and “hope of” is the ESV’s explanation. It may mean the steadfast love God would have shown them (the KJV has “forsake their own mercy”), or God himself, who can be called “my steadfast love” (Psalm 144:2), or less likely their own loyalty. The likely sense is the ESV’s: turning to idols means turning away from the only love that holds.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out upon the dry land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At God’s word the fish gives Jonah back to the dry land: an undignified rescue, but a real one, and a sign of Christ’s resurrection.

The LORD spoke to the fish. The fish obeys at once, which is more than the prophet did. Everything in this book does what God says except the man who knows him best.

It vomited Jonah out. The rescue is not dignified: Jonah is vomited onto the beach, filthy and half-drowned. God’s grace saves us; it does not flatter us. Many a rescued believer has begun again in an undignified heap, and it is still grace.

Upon the dry land. He lands on the very “dry land” he had confessed that God made (1:9), the place where obedience is possible again. God brings his servant back to the beginning, and in the next chapter the call will come a second time.

A sign of the Son of Man. Jesus made this chapter a sign of himself: “just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (Matthew 12:40). But hear the difference. Jonah prayed from the deep and was heard and lifted out. On the cross Jesus cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), and was not spared. He went down into death not for his own sin but for ours, and came up on the third day. Because he did, “Salvation belongs to the LORD” is not only something to admire but something we can have.

What, then, is the sign of Jonah? Jesus’ hearers demanded a miracle on request, and he said no sign would be given “except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matthew 12:39). Luke adds that “Jonah became a sign to the people of Nineveh” (Luke 11:30): a man as good as dead, brought back by God and standing in their streets with his word. The sign is not a wonder to watch but a person to hear: the risen Christ, back from death itself, still calls every generation to repent, and no greater sign will be given.

2.title: Salvation Belongs to the LORD
2.overview:
Where we are. Jonah has been thrown into the sea and swallowed by the fish God appointed (1:17). The runaway who would not pray on the ship now prays from the deep, and the first half of the book ends with him back on dry land.

The message. Salvation belongs to the LORD. When a person has gone as far down as it is possible to go, beyond any power to save himself, God hears his cry and brings him up. Grace reaches the disobedient prophet as surely as it reached the pagan sailors, and he contributes nothing to it but the cry for help.

Why it was said. Israel sang of a God who saves, and here one of its own prophets learns those songs again as a drowning man. The chapter also sets up the sting of chapter 4: the salvation Jonah celebrates for himself is the salvation he will resent for Nineveh (see the introduction).

How the chapter makes its case. From inside the fish Jonah thanks God that he called and was heard (vv. 1–2). He looks back on the descent: cast into the deep by God’s own hand, driven from his sight, shut in by waters, weeds and the bars of the world of the dead (vv. 3–6a). Then comes the reversal, “Yet you brought up my life from the pit”: as his life ebbed away he remembered the LORD, and his prayer reached the temple (vv. 6b–7). He confesses that idols forsake steadfast love, vows thanksgiving and sacrifice, and sums it all up: “Salvation belongs to the LORD!” (vv. 8–9). God speaks, the fish obeys, and Jonah lands where obedience can begin again (v. 10).

Where it leads. To Christ by pattern and contrast, on Jesus’ own authority (Matthew 12:40): a man goes down to the gates of death and is brought up again after three days. But Jonah went down for his own sin, cried out and was heard; Jesus went down for ours and cried, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46), and was not spared, so that everyone who calls from the depths might be. The chapter’s last cry is heaven’s too: “Salvation belongs to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb!” (Revelation 7:10).

For us. No one has sunk too far to pray, and no prayer from the depths is too late for God. Stop trying to climb out, and call on the one who has already gone down and come up for you. Then beware Jonah’s blind spot: it is possible to thank God sincerely for his mercy to us while holding on to the very grudge he means to deal with next.
2.theology:
God remains the God of his straying servant, and prayer reaches him from any depth (vv. 1-2, 7; Ps 18:6).

Believers may recognise God's hand behind the means that bring them low, without excusing anyone's sin (v. 3; Ps 42:7).

Faith speaks its "yet" when there is no evidence, trusting that God will not abandon his own (v. 4; Ps 31:22).

No one raises himself from the pit; salvation is God's work from first to last (v. 6; Ps 30:3; Eph 2:8-9).

Idols are empty, and those who trust them abandon the only steadfast love there is (v. 8).

Salvation belongs to the LORD, to give as he pleases, which is a comfort when it comes to us and a test when it comes to others (v. 9; Ps 3:8; Rev 7:10).

Jonah's three days in the deep are a sign of Christ, who went down into death for sinners and rose (vv. 1-10; Matt 12:40; Matt 27:46).
2.examples:
The man who would not pray on deck prays inside a fish, with seaweed wrapped round his head, and Israel's hymnbook gives him the words. Psalms learned in calm days are there for us in the dark.

One word, yet, turns his prayer around, and he gives thanks before the rescue arrives. Grace then saves him and leaves him in an undignified heap on the beach, which is still grace.

keyVerse.note: This cry is the centre of the whole book. Jonah learns it at the bottom of the sea, where he can contribute nothing, and the rest of the story tests whether he means it when the same salvation reaches Nineveh. Heaven sings it at the end, “to our God who sits on the throne, and to the Lamb” (Revelation 7:10).

2.reflection:
Jonah did not pray on the ship, but he prays from inside the fish. Why does it so often take a crisis to bring us to prayer, and how can we learn to pray before we reach the bottom?

Jonah’s prayer is woven from the Psalms. How has Scripture you learned in calmer days come back to you in hard times? What could you do now to store it up?

Jonah says “you cast me into the deep” (v. 3), though the sailors threw him. How can it comfort a believer in illness or loss that nothing reaches us except through God’s hand, without making God the author of evil?

“Salvation belongs to the LORD!” (v. 9). Where are you still trying to save yourself, by effort, achievement or religious performance? And what might it mean that Jonah could pray this beautiful prayer without once mentioning Nineveh?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — The Word a Second Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God does not discard the servant who failed; he sends him again with the same word. It comes “the second time”, the commission repeated almost exactly, with the added stress that Jonah is to preach the message God gives him (vv. 1–2). This time Jonah goes, into a city so large that it is “three days’ journey in breadth” (v. 3). A day into it he calls out the whole of his recorded sermon: forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown (v. 4). No promise of mercy is attached, yet the delay itself leaves room for one.
verseByVerse.theology: God gives his failed servant the same commission again, and this time he obeys.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to Jonah the second time, saying, "Arise, go to Nineveh, that great city, and call out against it the message that I tell you." So Jonah arose and went to Nineveh, according to the word of the LORD. Now Nineveh was an exceedingly great city, three days' journey in breadth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives his failed prophet the same commission a second time, and this time Jonah obeys and goes to the vast city.

The second time. Three words carry a world of grace. God could have found another prophet. Instead the same word comes to the same man.

The message that I tell you. The command is almost word for word what it was in 1:2, unsoftened, with one addition: “the message that I tell you”. Jonah is to preach God’s words, not his own. That is still every preacher’s calling, and a mercy: a messenger need not invent the message, only deliver it faithfully.

So Jonah arose and went to Nineveh. In chapter 1 he “rose to flee” (1:3); now he rises and obeys, a walk of several hundred miles.

An exceedingly great city. However the details are read (see below), it was vast, and God calls it great. He notices cities, their size, their trade, their cruelty and, as the book’s last verse shows, their people.

The God of second commissions. Peter denied Jesus three times, and the risen Christ asked him three times, “do you love me?”, and gave him his work back: “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17). The Lord who restored Peter is the God who sent Jonah again. A believer who has failed badly should read this verse slowly: failure is not the end of usefulness.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases in verse 3 are uncertain. The Hebrew calls Nineveh “a great city to God” (ESV note), which may mean great in God’s sight, or may simply be a way of saying “very great”. And “three days’ journey in breadth” may take in the whole district of Nineveh with its neighbouring towns (Genesis 10:11–12 calls Nineveh and the cities around it “the great city”), or, as the ESV also notes, may mean that a visit took three days. The walls of the city itself were later some 12 kilometres round. Either way, the sense is a huge city.
verseByVerse.note: Nineveh's walls, as later rebuilt by Sennacherib (about 700 BC), ran some 12 kilometres (7½ miles) around; "three days' journey" probably takes in the surrounding district too.

verseByVerse.quote: Jonah began to go into the city, going a day's journey. And he called out, "Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jonah’s whole recorded sermon is a single sentence of coming judgment, yet the forty days it allows are already a mercy.

Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown! That is the whole sermon, five words in Hebrew: no invitation, no promise of mercy, not even the name of the LORD.

Forty days. A short reprieve, and long enough to act. The word “overthrown” is the word used of Sodom and Gomorrah: God “overthrew those cities” (Genesis 19:25). Every hearer would know what that meant.

Threat and mercy. This is a real threat, not a bluff. Yet forty days’ notice is itself a mercy: a God who intended only destruction would say nothing at all.

The power of the word. See what God can do with a bare, reluctant sermon. The power is in the word of God, not in the eloquence or warmth of the man delivering it.

Isn’t warning people of judgment unloving? Many feel that love means accepting people as they are. But we do not think that anywhere else. A doctor who sees the tumour on the scan and talks only about the weather is not being kind; he is being negligent. A friend who watches you drive towards a washed-out bridge and keeps quiet is no friend. The question is never whether a warning is pleasant but whether it is true. Jonah’s few words were true, and they saved a city. And here is the gospel’s surprise: the God who sends the warning is the one who most wants it not to come true. He gave forty days because he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (Ezekiel 18:23), and in the end he did more than warn: he came himself and stood under the judgment he had announced. That is why a Christian warning, rightly given, should sound less like a threat and more like a rescue.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When people turn from their evil, God turns from the disaster he threatened. The people of Nineveh believe God and fast in sackcloth, from the greatest to the least (v. 5). The king himself leaves his throne for the ashes and decrees that the whole city, even its animals, fast, call out to God and turn from the violence in their hands, with no ground but the hope that God may relent (vv. 6–9). God sees not their sackcloth but their turning, and he does not bring the disaster (v. 10). The section shows both the power of God’s word and the mercy of his character.
verseByVerse.theology: God shows mercy to the worst of cities when they turn to him, and he has the right to do so.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people of Nineveh believed God. They called for a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least of them. The word reached the king of Nineveh, and he arose from his throne, removed his robe, covered himself with sackcloth, and sat in ashes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At one sentence from a foreign preacher, the whole city believes God and humbles itself, from the poorest to the king on his throne.

The people of Nineveh believed God. A pagan city, warned by a foreigner in one sentence, believed God, not merely Jonah.

They called for a fast and put on sackcloth. Their faith showed at once. Fasting and sackcloth, rough cloth worn in grief and humility, spread through rich and poor together, “from the greatest of them to the least of them”.

He arose from his throne. God’s word ran through the streets before it reached the palace (though the ESV notes that verse 6 may be read “had reached”, so the king may have heard it earlier). Then the most powerful man in the region gave up throne, robe and comfort for sackcloth and ashes. That is what repentance looks like when it reaches someone with something to lose.

Nineveh and Israel. Amos and Hosea preached for years in Israel, and Israel would not listen; one walk through Nineveh, and the city repents. Jesus made exactly this point: “The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41). It is possible to hear the gospel all our lives and be less moved than people who hear it once.

Did Nineveh really repent? The king is not named, and no surviving Assyrian record mentions it, but the records are incomplete, and kings recorded victories, not repentance. Revolts, plague and the eclipse of 763 BC may have left the city ready to listen (see the introduction); that is suggestive, not proof. Jesus treats the repentance as real (Matthew 12:41).

verseByVerse.quote: And he issued a proclamation and published through Nineveh, "By the decree of the king and his nobles: Let neither man nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything. Let them not feed or drink water, but let man and beast be covered with sackcloth, and let them call out mightily to God. Let everyone turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands. Who knows? God may turn and relent and turn from his fierce anger, so that we may not perish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The king calls the whole city to fast, pray and turn from its violence, claiming nothing and casting itself on the bare hope that God may relent.

By the decree of the king and his nobles. The king turns repentance into public policy. Even the animals fast in sackcloth, which sounds odd, but the point is complete seriousness: nothing in the city will carry on as normal while judgment hangs over it.

Call out mightily to God. This is more than emotion: they must pray in earnest, and “turn from his evil way and from the violence that is in his hands”. Repentance that stops at sackcloth is only a show. The Assyrians were famous for violence, and the king names it. Real repentance gets specific about what must stop, and it reaches the hands as well as the heart.

Who knows? The king claims nothing. He has no covenant, no promise, no Bible; he has heard a sentence of doom, and he throws himself on the possibility of mercy. Joel used the same words to Israel (Joel 2:14), and David said the same when his child was dying (2 Samuel 12:22). This is not doubt but humility. God’s mercy is never owed, and the one who says “Who knows?” and repents is far nearer to God’s heart than the one who assumes God must forgive.

Better than “Who knows?” The king had a rumour of mercy; we have the promise sealed at the cross: “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). So repentance is not a bargain to win mercy but a turning to the God who has already shown it in Christ, and the Holy Spirit, who gives repentance, is the one who changes what our hands do.

verseByVerse.quote: When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When God saw Nineveh turn from its evil, he turned from the disaster he had threatened, for his warnings are given so that people will repent.

When God saw what they did. What God saw was not the sackcloth but the turning: “how they turned from their evil way”. Their actions proved the repentance real.

The disaster that he had said he would do. The word for “disaster” is the same as Nineveh’s “evil” in 1:2 (ESV note): when the evil went, so did the disaster. When the King James Version says God “repented of the evil”, it does not mean he had done wrong, but that he turned from the harm he had threatened.

How can God change his mind? God tells us himself: “If at any time I declare concerning a nation or a kingdom, that I will pluck up and break down and destroy it, and if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it” (Jeremiah 18:7–8). A warning carries an unspoken condition, because it is given precisely so that people will turn.

God has not changed. The Ninevites changed, and God’s unchanging character, “gracious … and merciful, slow to anger” (4:2), means that his dealings with a repentant city must differ from his dealings with a violent one. A father who withholds a threatened punishment when his child stops has not become unreliable; he is being exactly who he always was. As God says through Ezekiel, “Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked … and not rather that he should turn from his way and live?” (Ezekiel 18:23).

What Jonah could not bear. This is the very thing Jonah could not bear, as the next chapter shows. He had God’s character exactly right, and that was what he could not stand.

A generation later. Nineveh’s repentance did not last for ever. A century or so later Nahum announced the city’s fall, and in 612 BC Nineveh was destroyed. One generation turned to God and was spared; its descendants returned to the old violence and were not. Each generation must repent for itself. The message has not changed, and it now comes with the good news of the Christ who bore the judgment: “repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15), for God “commands all people everywhere to repent” (Acts 17:30).

Where Christians differ. Open theists read verses like this to mean that God did not know how Nineveh would respond and changed his plans. Most Christians through history have held that God knows all things and his purposes do not change, so that “relenting” describes his real response to a change in people, seen from our side of the story.

This commentary’s view. God’s character and purpose did not change; Nineveh did. God ordained both the warning and the repentance it was meant to produce, and both the threat and the relenting were sincere, flowing from the same unchanging, merciful God.

3.title: The People of Nineveh Believed God
3.overview:
Where we are. The second half of the book opens exactly as the first did: “the word of the LORD came to Jonah” (1:1; 3:1). The runaway has been brought up from the deep and set on dry land, and God gives him the same commission again.

The message. God gives second chances, to his failed servant and to the worst of sinners. His word, even delivered in one bare sentence by a reluctant preacher, has power to turn a whole city. And when people turn from their evil, God turns from the judgment he threatened, because his warnings are given precisely so that people will repent.

Why it was said. Israel had heard prophet after prophet, Amos and Hosea among them, and would not turn (see the introduction). Here the most violent of the nations believes God at the first warning. The chapter shames a privileged people and shows how far God’s mercy is willing to reach.

How the chapter makes its case. The second commission (vv. 1–3): the same word comes again, and this time Jonah goes into the vast city. The sermon (v. 4): one sentence of judgment, with forty days to run. The response (vv. 5–9): the people believe God and fast, from the greatest to the least; the king leaves his throne for sackcloth and ashes and decrees prayer and a turning from violence, claiming nothing but “Who knows?” God’s answer (v. 10): he sees them turn, and he relents from the disaster.

Where it leads. To Christ first by the need it exposes. Jesus said that “The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here” (Matthew 12:41). If a pagan city turned at a reluctant prophet’s five Hebrew words, what of those who hear the Son of God himself? And by the character of God: the God who relents when sinners turn is the God who in Christ bore the judgment himself, so that the king’s anxious “Who knows?” becomes for us a sure promise of forgiveness to all who repent and believe.

For us. Failure is not the end of usefulness: the word comes a second time. No one is too far gone to repent, and no culture too hardened for God’s word. And real repentance is not sackcloth for show but turning from the evil in our own hands, to a God whose mercy we can now be certain of.
3.theology:
God restores failed servants and gives them their commission again (vv. 1-2; John 21:15-17).

Preachers are to deliver God's message, not their own, and God's word works even through a reluctant messenger (vv. 2, 4).

A warning of judgment is itself an act of mercy, since it is given so that people may turn (v. 4).

Saving faith shows itself in humility and action, and reaches the greatest and the least alike (vv. 5-6).

True repentance is specific: it turns from named sins, including violence, and it reaches the hands (v. 8).

Mercy can never be presumed upon; "Who knows?" is the right posture of a sinner before God (v. 9; Joel 2:14; 2 Sam 12:22).

God relents of threatened disaster when people turn, not because he changes, but because his unchanging character deals differently with the repentant (v. 10; Jer 18:7-8; Ezek 18:21-23).

Those who hear little and repent will condemn those who hear much and do not (v. 5; Matt 12:41; Luke 11:32).
3.examples:
A second call comes to a man who ran from the first, and he preaches a sermon of eight words with no mercy offered in it. Yet a whole city believes a foreign preacher it had no reason to trust. God's word does its work even through a reluctant messenger.

A king steps off his throne and sits down in the ashes, and even the cattle wear sackcloth, because nothing can carry on as normal. A pagan asks "Who knows?" and finds out that God is merciful. No one who turns to him is too far gone.

keyVerse.quote: When God saw what they did, how they turned from their evil way, God relented of the disaster that he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.
keyVerse.note: This verse is the hinge of the book. The evil that came up before God in 1:2 is gone, and so is the disaster it deserved, because God’s warnings are meant to be heeded. It is the mercy Jonah feared and the mercy every sinner needs, and it reaches its fullness at the cross, where the judgment was not simply withdrawn but borne.

3.reflection:
The word came to Jonah “the second time” (v. 1). How have you experienced God’s patience after failure? How might this verse change the way we treat a fellow believer who has failed badly?

Jonah’s sermon was one sentence, yet a city repented. What does this teach about where the power of preaching and witness lies, and how should it encourage those who feel they have little to offer?

The king named the violence in their hands (v. 8). Why does real repentance need to be specific? What might “the violence that is in his hands” look like in a modern life?

The Ninevites had only “Who knows?” (v. 9); Christians have the promise of forgiveness in Christ (1 John 1:9). How should that certainty shape the way we repent, and the way we speak to others about turning to God?
