verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Prophet Who Wanted a Funeral
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The prophet who received mercy cannot bear to see it given to his enemies. When Nineveh is spared, Jonah is exceedingly displeased, and at last he says why he ran: he knew God was gracious, merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and he did not want that love to reach Nineveh (vv. 1–2). He asks to die rather than live in such a world (v. 3). God does not strike him down but asks a question: “Do you do well to be angry?” (v. 4). Jonah gives no answer. He goes out east of the city and sits in a rough shelter, waiting to see whether it will be destroyed after all (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: It is possible to know God's character perfectly and resent it.

verseByVerse.quote: But it displeased Jonah exceedingly, and he was angry. And he prayed to the LORD and said, "O LORD, is not this what I said when I was yet in my country? That is why I made haste to flee to Tarshish; for I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love, and relenting from disaster. Therefore now, O LORD, please take my life from me, for it is better for me to die than to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jonah is furious that God has spared Nineveh, and admits that he ran because he knew God is gracious and did not want that grace for his enemies.

It displeased Jonah exceedingly. A whole city has been saved, and the preacher is furious. The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads “it was exceedingly evil to Jonah”, the book’s word for Nineveh’s evil in 1:2. The evil has gone out of Nineveh and reappeared in the prophet’s heart. That devastating turn is the point of the chapter.

Why Jonah ran. At last we learn why he fled. It was not fear of Assyrian soldiers or doubt about his calling. He ran because he was afraid God would forgive them.

For I knew that you are a gracious God. He quotes the description of himself that God gave to Moses, to which the Old Testament returns again and again: “The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). Israel sang it (Psalm 103:8) and other prophets preached it (Joel 2:13). Jonah can recite it word for word, and he hates it when it is applied to the wrong people.

Behind his anger. We are not told everything behind it. He may have feared what Assyria would later do to his own country, which did happen. He may have felt that mercy to such a violent city was an offence against justice. He may simply have wanted to be right about the judgment he had announced. What the text says plainly is that he knew what God was like and could not bear it.

Please take my life from me. Elijah and Moses once asked God to take their lives (1 Kings 19:4; Numbers 11:15), crushed by the burden of ministry, and God met Elijah’s despair with sleep, bread and “the sound of a low whisper” (1 Kings 19:5–12). Jonah’s case is different. He is in a temper: he would rather be dead than live in a world where God forgives Nineveh. Anger of that kind shrinks a person’s world until it holds nothing but himself and his grievance.

What grace is. Jonah calls God “a gracious God”, and we tend to hear grace as niceness, God being pleasant to pleasant people. In the Bible it is favour given to people who have earned the opposite, and that is exactly what Jonah cannot stomach. Timothy Keller often pointed out, most fully in The Prodigal Prophet, that Jonah plays both sons in Jesus’ parable: in chapter 1 he runs from the Father like the younger brother, and here he stands outside sulking like the elder one. Underneath the sulk is a heart leaning on its own record and its people’s standing; if God’s favour is free, Jonah has no edge over anyone, which is why grace offends good people more than bad ones. The gospel turns this inside out. Jonah was brought up from the deep when he deserved to drown (2:9–10), and Christ went down into the deep of God’s judgment so that grace could reach Ninevites and Jonahs alike: “by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8). See also Grace in the Theological Dictionary.

The test for us. Most of us are glad that God is merciful to us and to people like us. The test comes when he shows mercy to someone who has hurt us, or to a group we have written off. Jesus faced exactly this: “This man receives sinners and eats with them”, grumbled the religious people (Luke 15:2), and he answered with the story of a father and two sons, one of whom would not come in to the party (Luke 15:28). People who know they live on free favour can be glad when it falls on someone else. This week that may mean praying by name for the person whose blessing you most resent.

If life feels not worth living. If you have ever felt that, take heart: God was gentle with the crushed Elijah and with the angry Jonah, and he let neither man go. Such feelings are real and call for help: from God in prayer, from the church, and from a biblical counsellor, who will also ask for a medical check-up so that any bodily cause is found and treated; medicine, where it is needed, is no failure of faith. Anyone thinking of ending their life should tell someone today, a pastor, a doctor, a friend or a crisis line, and in an emergency get help the same day.
verseByVerse.note: Jonah adds relenting from disaster to Exodus 34:6, as Joel 2:13 does: the very mercy Nineveh has just received (3:10).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said, "Do you do well to be angry?" Jonah went out of the city and sat to the east of the city and made a booth for himself there. He sat under it in the shade, till he should see what would become of the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God answers his angry prophet with a gentle question, and Jonah, refusing to answer, sits outside the city hoping to watch it destroyed.

Do you do well to be angry? God does not strike Jonah down. He asks a question, as a patient teacher does, inviting him to examine his own heart. He deals with his sulking servants far more gently than they deserve, and his questions call for an honest answer. When we are angry with God, the way back is not to pretend otherwise but to let him ask us why.

Jonah went out of the city. Jonah does not answer. He walks out, builds a rough shelter east of the city, and sits down “till he should see what would become of the city”. He is hoping the fire will fall after all; the forty days may not yet be over, and he means to have a good view. Picture it: a man of God in the shade, waiting for a city of more than a hundred thousand people to be destroyed. It is an ugly image, and Scripture does not soften it.

The god who hates the people we hate. Jonah is not the only one who has wanted a god like that. The writer Anne Lamott, in Bird by Bird, passes on a friend’s remark that you can safely assume you have created God in your own image when it turns out that God hates all the same people you do. The test catches almost everybody: the religious version of that god despises the immoral, the secular version despises the bigots, and Jonah’s would have been a patriot, a reliable friend of Israel’s national interest. But a god who always agrees with us is only ourselves enlarged, and he can never surprise us, rebuke us or save us. The real God sits Jonah down on that hillside and refuses to share his hatred. That is uncomfortable, and also the best news Jonah could have: a God who could love Nineveh could love a sulking prophet. He loved us “while we were enemies” (Romans 5:10), and that love is the only thing that ever dissolves our own hostility.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–11 — The Plant, the Worm and the Question
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God exposes what Jonah really loves, and asks whether his own compassion is not right. He appoints a plant to shade Jonah, and the prophet is exceedingly glad; then a worm kills the plant, and a scorching wind and the sun bring him to ask for death again (vv. 6–8). Asked whether he does well to be angry about the plant, Jonah insists that he does (v. 9). God’s reply is the book’s conclusion: you pity a plant you did not make; should I not pity a great city of more than 120,000 people, and its animals, which I made? (vv. 10–11). The book ends there, with God’s question left unanswered.
verseByVerse.theology: God's compassion for people who do not yet know him is greater than his servant's, and the book ends by asking whether we share it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the LORD God appointed a plant and made it come up over Jonah, that it might be a shade over his head, to save him from his discomfort. So Jonah was exceedingly glad because of the plant. But when dawn came up the next day, God appointed a worm that attacked the plant, so that it withered. When the sun rose, God appointed a scorching east wind, and the sun beat down on the head of Jonah so that he was faint. And he asked that he might die and said, "It is better for me to die than to live."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God gives Jonah a plant and then takes it away, to show him that he cares more for his own comfort than for a city full of people.

The LORD God appointed a plant. God “appointed” again, as he appointed the fish (1:17), this time a plant that shades Jonah’s head and saves him from his “discomfort” (the ESV notes this may be read “his evil”, the same word again).

Exceedingly glad because of the plant. This is the only time the book says Jonah was glad. He was exceedingly angry about a city being saved and exceedingly glad about a bush that kept the sun off his head. That is a portrait of a heart out of shape, and it is meant to make us uncomfortable, for it is easy to care more about a comfortable life than about people who are perishing.

God appointed a worm. Then God appoints a worm, and a scorching east wind, the dry desert wind that drains the strength out of a person. The God who commands great fish and great cities also commands a worm and a breeze. Nothing is too large or too small for his purposes.

It is better for me to die than to live. So, a second time, Jonah asks to die (see the note on vv. 1–3). This is not God taking petty revenge on a sulking prophet; it is a lesson carefully prepared. God takes away the comfort to expose what Jonah loves, and to give him what he needs far more than shade: a heart that cares as God cares.

Uncertain wording. The plant’s name, qiqayon, occurs only here. The castor-oil plant (ESV note), fast-growing and broad-leaved, is the likeliest guess; older versions have “gourd”, and when Jerome put “ivy” in his Latin translation, Augustine reported that it caused an uproar in a North African congregation. The word translated “scorching” is also rare, and its exact sense (scorching, sultry or still) is not certain. Neither uncertainty touches the lesson.
verseByVerse.note: The plant (Hebrew qiqayon) was probably the castor-oil plant (ESV note), which grows fast and has broad leaves.

verseByVerse.quote: But God said to Jonah, "Do you do well to be angry for the plant?" And he said, "Yes, I do well to be angry, angry enough to die." And the LORD said, "You pity the plant, for which you did not labor, nor did you make it grow, which came into being in a night and perished in a night. And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s last word is a question: if Jonah pities a plant he never made, should not God pity a great city of people and animals that he made?

Do you do well to be angry for the plant? God repeats his question from verse 4, now with the plant in it. This time Jonah answers, defiantly, sure he is in the right. That is what anger does: it supplies its own certainty. God’s reply is an argument, and it is unanswerable.

You pity the plant. Jonah pitied a plant he had not planted or grown, which came and went overnight and meant nothing to him but shade. How much more should God pity Nineveh, a city of men, women and children whom he made and has kept alive every day of their lives, and whose wickedness he has seen (1:2) without ceasing to care for them. Jonah grieves for a bush and would gladly watch a multitude burn. These are people in the dark, and God’s heart goes out to them.

And also much cattle? The book’s last words are almost comical and entirely serious: the God Jonah serves cares about everything he has made.

The unanswered question. The book ends with a question, and we never hear Jonah’s answer. The silence is deliberate. It was aimed first at Israel, called to be a light to the nations and sulking instead, and it is aimed now at every reader. Do we share God’s compassion for people who do not know their right hand from their left? Or are we more upset about our comforts than about their destruction?

A greater than Jonah. The final word belongs to Jesus. A greater than Jonah came to a city that would not listen, and instead of sitting on a hill waiting for it to burn, “he wept over it” (Luke 19:41). He did not preach one grudging sentence and withdraw; he “suffered outside the gate” to make his people holy through his own blood (Hebrews 13:12). Jonah was thrown into the storm for his own sin, and lived; Christ went into the storm of judgment for other people’s sin, and died. And he did it for enemies: “while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Why the church has a mission. That is why the church has a mission rather than a grievance, and why the love of Christ, poured into us by his Spirit, makes us willing to go to our own Ninevehs. Heaven’s song is sung to a Lamb who was slain and who “ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9): Nineveh’s kind of people, and ours. The book stops at a question mark, and the answer has to come from the reader’s life.

Who are the 120,000 who do not know right from left? Some take them to be small children, which would mean a much larger city besides. The likelier reading is the whole population, ignorant of God’s law: people who cannot tell right from wrong because nobody has ever taught them. Small children are certainly among them, and God cares for them all, and for the animals too. It is a tender thought that God’s eye was on the little ones of a cruel city, who had no share in its violence. When Nineveh finally fell, in Nahum’s day, children surely suffered with it; this verse tells us that God is never indifferent to a single one of them.
verseByVerse.note: The Hebrew says "more than twelve ten-thousands", a round and very large number for an ancient city.

4.title: And Should Not I Pity Nineveh?
4.overview:
Where we are. Nineveh has repented and God has relented (3:10). The story could have ended there, with a city saved; instead it turns to the prophet, and the last chapter is about Jonah’s heart.

The message. God’s mercy is larger than his servant’s heart, and he means to enlarge that heart. Jonah is furious that the gracious God he knows has been gracious to his enemies. God answers him not with judgment but with patient questions and an object lesson, and ends with a question that asks every reader whether we share his compassion for people who do not know their right hand from their left.

Why it was said. Israel, like Jonah, knew God’s covenant mercy and wanted it kept for themselves while their enemies were punished (see the introduction). The open ending was aimed first at them, and through them at every believer who is glad of grace for himself but not for others.

How the chapter makes its case. Jonah’s anger (vv. 1–3): displeased “exceedingly”, he quotes God’s own description of himself as the reason he ran, and asks to die. God’s question and Jonah’s vigil (vv. 4–5): asked, “Do you do well to be angry?”, Jonah does not answer, but sits east of the city hoping to see it destroyed after all. The object lesson (vv. 6–8): God appoints a plant, a worm and a scorching wind, and the prophet who was furious at a city’s rescue is overjoyed at a little shade and in despair at its loss. The final question (vv. 9–11): if Jonah pities a plant he did not make, should not God pity a great city of people and animals that he did?

Where it leads. To Christ by the character of God revealed in him, and by contrast. The gracious God of verse 2 is seen in full in Jesus, who came to a city that rejected him and “wept over it” (Luke 19:41), then died for his enemies. Jonah sat outside the city waiting for judgment to fall on others; Jesus “suffered outside the gate” (Hebrews 13:12) and let it fall on himself. And Jesus told the story Jonah is living, of an elder brother who would not go in to the feast, and a father who came out and pleaded with him (Luke 15:28).

For us. Ask whose blessing you would resent, and whether you are more upset to lose your comforts than you are about others perishing. People who know they live on free grace can be glad when it falls on someone else, even an enemy. The book ends with a question mark, and our lives write the answer.
4.theology:
A person may know God's character exactly and still resent it when it is shown to others (vv. 1-2; Exod 34:6).

Anger at God’s mercy is the sin of the elder brother in Jesus’ parable of the lost son, and it is found among religious people (vv. 1-3; Luke 15:1-2, 28-32).

God has compassion on people who are ignorant of him, and on his whole creation (v. 11; Matt 5:44-45).

The one greater than Jonah wept over a city and suffered outside the gate for his enemies (vv. 5, 11; Luke 19:41; Heb 13:12; Rom 5:8-10; Matt 12:41).

The book's closing question is left unanswered so that the reader must answer it (v. 11; Rev 5:9).
4.examples:
Jonah 4 shows a preacher furious that his sermon worked, reciting the Bible’s great description of God’s mercy as a complaint, and then sitting in a shelter on the hillside in the hope that fire will fall after all.

God teaches him with a worm at dawn and a scorching wind at sunrise. Jonah was exceedingly angry about a city and exceedingly glad about a bush; he pitied a plant that cost him nothing and felt nothing for a hundred thousand people. What we grieve over and what we celebrate still show what we love.

The book ends with a question and no reply, because the reply belongs to us.

keyVerse.quote: And should not I pity Nineveh, that great city, in which there are more than 120,000 persons who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle?
keyVerse.note: The book ends not with Jonah’s answer but with God’s question, and the reader is left to answer it. It reveals the heart of the God who made Nineveh and would not let it perish without warning and mercy. That compassion stands in full view in Jesus, who wept over the city that rejected him and died for his enemies.

4.reflection:
Jonah ran because he knew God is “gracious … and merciful, slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love” (v. 2). Is there anyone, or any kind of person, you would be uncomfortable to see God bless or forgive? Why?

God answers Jonah’s anger with questions rather than punishment (vv. 4, 9). What do his questions show about how God deals with his people when they are angry, and how might we answer “Do you do well to be angry?” honestly?

Jonah was exceedingly glad about a plant and exceedingly angry about a city’s rescue (vv. 1, 6). What are the “plants” in our lives, the comforts we would grieve more than the lost? How can we tell when our heart is out of shape?

The book ends with God’s question unanswered (v. 11). How would you answer it, and what would that answer look like this month in your attitude to the people you find hardest to love?
